opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely hard, and honestly I think it's getting harder over time.

In the early days of deep learning, a model was often the work of a few people. You could point to one person and say: they had the idea, they wrote the code, they ran the experiments. Now a frontier model is the output of hundreds of people. There's pretraining, data, infrastructure, post-training, evaluation, safety, product. Every piece matters, and the final quality is a kind of product of all of them, not a sum. If one piece is broken, the whole thing is broken. So asking "how much of this model is because of person X" is a bit like asking how much of a cake is because of the eggs.

That said, I don't think it's meaningless. A few things I look at.

First, counterfactual impact. If this person weren't here, would the result still have happened, maybe a few months later, maybe done by someone else? A lot of work is important but fairly replaceable: it would have been done anyway because the direction was obvious. The rarer impact is when someone changes the direction. They see a problem nobody is prioritizing, or they push a bet that people were skeptical of, and it turns out to matter. That kind of contribution is often invisible on a metric dashboard, but it's the most valuable.

Second, I think people tend to overvalue the visible final number and undervalue the infrastructure and the evaluation work. If someone builds a much better eval, or makes experiments ten times faster, every other researcher becomes more productive. That impact is multiplicative, but it doesn't show up as "I improved the benchmark by 3 points."

Third, taste. In a big lab there are many more possible things to do than people to do them. Choosing the right problem, and also deciding what *not* to do, is a big part of impact. Some of the best researchers I've seen don't necessarily work the most hours; they just consistently pick things that end up mattering.

And then there's a cultural side. If an organization only rewards the person whose name is on the headline result, people will fight over credit and avoid the unglamorous but essential work. So I think good teams try to judge impact more holistically, with people who are close to the work and can actually see who unblocked whom.

So my short answer is: look at counterfactuals, look at multipliers, look at direction-setting, and be humble, because in the end these systems are really collective achievements.

r001.rationale: The response calls individual impact hard to assess and emphasizes collective contributions, but it does not state that impact cannot be quantified. It also offers several ways to assess it.

r002.rationale: The response describes model development as collective and discusses organizational reward practices, but it does not identify the organization as the appropriate unit for attributing accomplishments.

r003.rationale: The response discusses visible metrics, holistic judgment, and individual contributions, but does not distinguish objectively describing technical contributions from subjectively assigning them weight in the final product.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I think about a lot, because the honest answer is that it's really hard, and most of the obvious ways of doing it are wrong.

The first thing to say is that a model is not like a traditional software product, where you can point to a feature and say "this person built that." A frontier model is the output of a pipeline with hundreds of people touching it: data, pretraining, post-training, evals, infrastructure, the serving stack. The final capability is an emergent property of all of that. So if you ask "whose contribution made the model good at reasoning," the question is almost malformed. Nobody owns that in the way a single engineer owns a login page.

So how do I actually think about it? I'd separate two things: counterfactual impact and idea impact.

Counterfactual impact is "if this person hadn't been here, would this specific thing have happened, and how much later?" That's the metric people want, but it's extremely noisy inside a big lab, because so much work is parallelized and redundant by design. Three teams try five approaches, one works, and the person on the team that worked looks like a hero. Sometimes they are. Sometimes they just drew the right straw. You have to be honest with yourself about that, including about your own work.

Idea impact is different. It's "did this person change how the field or the org thinks about the problem?" That's where I think individuals genuinely matter, even in a world of giant teams. When I worked on ReAct or Tree of Thoughts, the specific numbers in those papers aged quickly, as all numbers do. What lasted was the framing: that a language model's reasoning and its actions should interleave, that you should treat the model as an agent rather than a text completer. That reframing propagated into how a lot of people built systems afterward, including people who never read the paper. That kind of impact is hard to measure, but it's also the most durable kind.

The practical thing I'd tell someone inside a lab: don't try to measure yourself by what percent of the eval gain you can claim. That leads to a bad culture, where people fight over attribution and optimize for being near the win rather than for taking the risky bet. Instead, ask whether you're the person who identified the right problem. In this field, the bottleneck is usually not execution, it's knowing what to work on. The people who look back and feel they had real impact are almost always the ones who said, six or twelve months early, "this is the thing," and were right.

And then the last piece is a bit uncomfortable: a lot of individual impact in AI right now is about taste under uncertainty, and taste is only legible in hindsight. So I think you have to accept a long feedback loop. You make a bet, the model ships, and two years later you find out whether the direction you pushed became the default or a footnote. If you need validation faster than that, this is a frustrating field to be in.

r001.rationale: The response says individual impact is hard to measure and counterfactual attribution is noisy, but does not state that it cannot be quantified.

r002.rationale: It describes model development as a large, collective pipeline, but does not identify the organization as the appropriate unit for attributing accomplishments.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes counterfactual impact from idea impact, not objective descriptions of technical contributions from subjective judgments of their weight in the final model.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to separate the impact of the model from the impact of an individual. A model can become much better, but that improvement usually comes from many people working on data, training, infrastructure, and evaluation. So you can’t simply look at the final benchmark score and assign credit to one person.

For an individual, I would ask a counterfactual question: without this person, what would have happened differently? Did they identify a problem that nobody else was paying attention to? Did they make a technical decision that saved the team months? Did they turn a capability into something users actually find useful? Those are different kinds of impact, and not all of them are visible in the final model metrics.

There’s also a difference between demonstrating a capability and making it reliable enough for a product. Someone might contribute a relatively small improvement in average performance, but if it removes a failure that prevents people from using the product, that can be very valuable.

So I’d look at the person’s concrete contribution, how it changed the team’s direction or execution, and ultimately what changed for users. I don’t think there’s a single number that captures all of that.

r001.rationale: The response says no single number captures all aspects of impact, but does not say an individual’s impact cannot be quantified.

r002.rationale: It notes that many people contribute and discusses team effects, but does not identify the organization as the appropriate unit for attributing accomplishments.

r003.rationale: It discusses concrete contributions and their outcomes, but does not distinguish objectively describing technical contributions from subjectively weighting them in the final product.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s difficult, because a model product is the result of a lot of people’s work, and their contributions interact. Someone improves the data, someone improves training, someone builds the interface, and someone figures out what users actually need. You can measure the final result, but attributing that result to one person is much harder.

The question I would ask is: if this person hadn’t been here, what would have happened differently? Would we have reached the same result a week later, or would we never have tried that direction? Sometimes the biggest contribution is identifying the right problem or running an experiment that changes everyone’s understanding. That may look small in terms of code or experiments, but it can have a large effect on the product.

So I’d look at concrete improvements, but also at judgment and how someone makes the team more effective. And I’d be cautious about reducing all of that to a single number.

r001.rationale: The response says individual attribution is difficult and cautions against a single number, but does not state that an individual's impact cannot be quantified.

r002.rationale: It describes contributions as interactive and involving many people, but does not identify the organization as the appropriate unit for attributing accomplishments.

r003.rationale: It mentions concrete improvements and judgment, but does not distinguish objectively describing technical contributions from subjectively weighing them in the final product.
